transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-29
Time: 11:00 PT / 14:00 ET
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: Enabled

Attendees: Jordan Hale (Redwood AE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE), Liam Torres (Head of ML, Acme Retail), Nina Park (PM), Marco Ruiz (SRE), Sofia Alvarez (Data Scientist)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Quick walkthrough of Redwood Eval / Optimize features focused on prompt sets, regression alerts, and A/B playback. Covered API snippets, Console demo of prompt sets, and a live A/B playback scenario. Discussed pilot logistics, security requirements (SOC2, KMS), and benchmarks (latency vs cost).

Topics Covered:
- Setting up prompt sets and labeling criteria
- Running A/B playback and paired comparisons
- Regression alerts and thresholds, SLA considerations
- API vs Console workflows for automation
- Pilot scoping and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll—uh—kick us off. Jordan from Redwood, AE. Priya from the SE team will do the bulk of the product walk. Welcome, Acme team.
[00:18] Liam: Hey thanks Jordan, excited to see how your eval tooling can fit into our QA pipeline. We have a big push to roll out a new product recommendation assistant in Q3, and quality regressions have been a headache.
[00:32] Priya: Great, yeah we'll show the prompt sets flow, the playback A/B compare, and how regression alerts trigger. Quick ask: what does your current stack look like for model serving? Hosted or self-hosted?
[00:45] Nina: We're on a mix. For production we use our in-house model server for latency-critical endpoints, but we also evaluate third-party hosted models for experimentation. So we want both API hooks and console-level playbooks.
[00:58] Marco: Security wise, we need to know about VPC peering, KMS integration, and audit logs. We have stringent logging retention.
[01:10] Priya: Totally understood—those are all things Redwood supports. We have SOC2 and ISO summaries I'll share, KMS integration for private deployments, and per-request audit logs. We'll include the network diagram in the follow-up.
[01:25] Sofia: From an evaluation angle, our biggest pain is regression noise. We often see small prompt changes cause large NPS drop in user tests. Curious how you do signal-to-noise filtering.
[01:38] Priya: Good question. The Eval/Optimize stack uses paired A/B comparisons and configurable regression thresholds. You can build prompt sets that are grouped by intent and then define custom metrics—semantic similarity, intent classification accuracy, or user-defined scoring. We also support paired statistical tests for significance.
[01:57] Jordan: Quick roadmap note—Priya will show the Console, and then we'll switch to a short API notebook we prepared which runs an A/B playback across a sample prompt set.

[02:12] Priya: Ok I'm sharing my screen. This is the Redwood Console—home -> Eval -> Prompt Sets. Here's a prompt set we imported for a retail FAQ example. See the columns: prompt text, expected label, baseline model response, and pass/fail rules.
[02:35] (screen noise)
[02:40] Priya: The import supports csv or via API. You can tag prompts for cohorts—like high-value customers, mobile users, or long-tail queries. Tagging is useful to create separate baselines and alerting.
[02:53] Nina: Can we restrict who can edit those prompt sets? We have a small ML ops team that should be the gatekeepers.
[03:05] Priya: Yep, RBAC in the Console—roles for viewer, editor, approver. Approver is required for rolling a new baseline. Also audit trail shows who changed which prompt and when.
[03:20] Marco: Nice. Do you store the prompt text in a way that's encrypted at rest? We can't have raw PII stored unencrypted.
[03:30] Priya: All stored data is encrypted at rest, and in Private deployments you can plug in your own KMS. We also support tokenization or redaction during ingestion if you want to avoid storing PII fields.

[03:44] Priya: Now, Alerts. You can set up regression alerts on metric thresholds—absolute or relative to baseline. Example: if accept_rate drops by 5% and p-value < 0.05, we create an incident and notify via Slack, PagerDuty, or email.
[04:00] Liam: Do you support rolling windows? We look at 24h and 7d windows to separate transient noise from real regressions.
[04:10] Priya: Yes, alerting supports rolling windows, and you can configure minimum sample size, lookback period, and the test type. We also have noise-reduction options like smoothing and outlier removal.

[04:28] Priya: Switching to A/B playback—this is where you take a prompt set and replay it against two model variants. The console shows side-by-side responses and a paired comparison view with difference highlights.
[04:42] (typing)
[04:46] Priya: I'll run a small playback now—using our sample retail prompts. It will call the Redwood API in the background; you can also run this via our Python SDK.
[05:00] [05:00] (playback running)
[05:20] Priya: Ok results populating. You can see the per-prompt delta, an aggregate score, and a significance test. We also auto-generate a list of candidate regressions sorted by effect size.
[05:38] Sofia: Does it surface hallucinations specifically? We need to know when a response invents facts.
[05:47] Priya: We have a hallucination detector heuristic—it flags high-confidence factual assertions with low grounding score. You can plug in a custom checker too; many customers use a knowledge-base recall metric.

[06:02] Jordan: Quick aside—many teams ask about latency tradeoffs when running these checks in production vs offline. For playback and heavy evals we recommend offline batches. For simple guardrail checks (e.g., flagging profanity), use lightweight runtime checks in the API path.
[06:18] Marco: For the pilot, are you suggesting we run playback on our staging model instances or use Redwood-hosted snapshots?
[06:30] Priya: Either works. For initial proof-of-value we often do hosted playback to measure model variant differences quickly. For security-sensitive enterprises you can use Private deployment where Redwood's agent runs the playback inside your VPC and never leaves.

[06:47] Priya: I'll drop a quick API snippet in chat—this is a Python pseudocode example that runs an A/B playback via the SDK.
[06:55] (chat note: link to gist of a small notebook)
[07:02] Priya: Code excerpt:
    from redwood import EvalClient
    client = EvalClient(api_key=STAGING_KEY)
    client.run_playback(prompt_set_id="ps-123", variants=["model-v1","model-v2"], metrics=["exact_match","semantic_sim"], batch_size=50)

[07:25] Nina: That looks easy enough. How long to run a meaningful sample? We have about 10k unique prompts but many are low-traffic.
[07:36] Priya: For paired stats, a few hundred to a couple thousand prompts is often sufficient depending on effect size. We'll help you pick a statistically defensible sample.

[07:50] Liam: Can the platform also help with triage? We need categorization like "regression due to prompt drift" or "model degradation" vs "data distribution shift".
[08:03] Priya: We have automated triage heuristics—if the failure modes correlate with particular prompt tags or user cohorts, we surface that. We also link to the raw logs and request traces so SREs can filter by tokenization, latency, or resource errors.

[08:20] Marco: Speaking of latency, any overhead for adding instrumentation? If we add a pre-response checker we can't add more than ~50ms on p99.
[08:31] Jordan: Important point—Instrumentation for deep evals runs offline. Inline guardrails are lightweight and purpose-built. For heavier semantic checks you run them asynchronously and route fallback responses if issues detected.

[08:50] Priya: Switching back to Console—here's the regression dashboard. You can see historical trendlines, cohort breakdowns, and active alerts. There's also an experiments tab for A/B split routing and automatic rollbacks if a threshold breaches during canary.
[09:07] Sofia: Do you support automatic rollback to a pinned baseline model? We sometimes need immediate reversion if live quality drops.
[09:18] Priya: Yes—canary + automatic fallback. The routing policy can be configured to shift traffic back to a safe model variant or a cached baseline if error rates spike.

[09:33] Priya: Now a quick live demo of alert config—I'll create a rule: cohort = "high_value", metric = "accept_rate", condition = "relative_drop > 4% over 24h", notify = Slack channel #ml-alerts.
[09:50] (clicks)
[09:55] Priya: Save and activate. When a playback runs and the threshold is breached, it will show up in the incident feed.

[10:05] Nina: Can we tune alert sensitivity per cohort? For long-tail cohorts we want looser thresholds.
[10:13] Priya: Absolutely. Cohort-level thresholds are the recommended approach.

[10:22] Liam: Alright, curious about cost. How do you bill for eval runs? Per token? Per request? Flat?
[10:33] Jordan: For hosted Eval we've got a usage model—per-eval call which is roughly proportional to token compute used during playback. For Dedicated/Private customers we offer bulk packages and committed capacity which drops unit cost. We'll send pricing examples.

[10:49] Marco: Are there any examples of customers who run nightly playback jobs as part of CI? We want to automate regression checks on every model commit.
[10:58] Priya: Yes, teams do nightly CI-driven playback. We integrate with CI systems via the API and can run incremental playbacks against changed prompt sets. The Console also exposes a scheduler API.

[11:12] (quiet)
[11:20] Priya: Ok switching to the notebook playback—I'll show the Python output that ranks items by effect size. Note some transcripts may have imperfect recognition here—ignore minor typos.
[11:38] Priya: Here, line item—prompt id 482: model-v2 introduces a polite but incorrect product attribute. It's flagged as suspected hallucination; confidence 0.86.
[11:52] Sofia: Can we attach a human review workflow from that flag? Like route to SME for labeling and then re-run stats?
[12:02] Priya: Yes, you can push flagged prompts to a review queue inside the Console. Reviewers can annotate outcomes and we store those as ground truth for future runs.

[12:18] Jordan: Brief commercial note—for pilots we usually provision a sandbox account, attach a staging key, and walk through a 2–4 week test. After that, we review metrics and propose dedicated capacity if needed.
[12:33] Liam: Sounds good. What about compliance? We operate in EU and need data residency.
[12:42] Jordan: Redwood Private supports regional deployments, you can host control plane in your VPC or choose regional hosting. We'll share the data residency options and legal addenda.

[12:55] Nina: I saw mention of auto-labeling in the docs—how reliable is that? We have limited reviewer bandwidth.
[13:05] Priya: Auto-labeling uses heuristics and model-assisted labeling—helpful for triage but we recommend human verification for final ground truth, especially on high-impact cohorts.

[13:18] (typing)
[13:22] Priya: Ok last piece—integration points. You can call the Eval API directly from your CI, or use event-based triggers in the Console to kick off a playback when a new model is deployed. There's also a webhook connector for Slack/JIRA.
[13:38] Marco: For our SREs, do you provide traces to link back to infra metrics? We need to correlate a quality drop with GPU OOMs or increased latency.
[13:48] Priya: Yes, we surface request-level metadata—latency, node id, kernel errors—and expose those in the incident view so you can correlate with Prometheus metrics.

[14:00] Jordan: Ok let's recap quick and assign next steps. Jordan will send security docs. Priya will prepare the demo notebook and sample A/B notebook link. Acme to provide prompt set and specify success criteria. We'll plan a pilot kickoff in the next two weeks.
[14:18] Liam: Thanks everyone, this was helpful. We'll sync internally and get the prompt set out.
[14:25] Nina: One last micro-question—are there built-in report exports for exec-level summaries? We need PDF exports for weekly reviews.
[14:35] Priya: Yep, you can export PDF/CSV and schedule weekly digests.
[14:40] Jordan: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up over email with the artifacts.
[14:45] (meeting ends)
